Institutional baselines improved (respect for oversight, apolitical DOJ posture), yet Court doctrine and structural incentives from the 2010s persisted. Week 0 weights these durable architectures over goodwill. Difficulty 1.4 is sticky: norms can shift quickly, but doctrine, infrastructure, and political economy create drag on full repair. Week 0 leaves runway for four years of movement. Adjusted by decree and agreement to correct unrealistic baseline calibration.

traits.trait_name: Memory is curated by power—what cannot be controlled is erased

institutional_shifts: The Supreme Court dramatically expanded presidential removal power over independent agencies (Trump v. Slaughter), overturning 90 years of precedent and enabling politicization of regulatory bodies, even as it simultaneously protected Fed independence procedurally and struck down the birthright citizenship order.

Congress remains largely gridlocked and reactive: Speaker Johnson warned of Democratic 'revenge' oversight, a Republican senator (Cassidy) publicly rebuked Trump for treating Congress as an 'appendage,' and the NDAA was blocked by intra-party disputes over unrelated voter-ID provisions.

The White House built parallel, unaccountable digital infrastructure (National Design Studio) handling passports, voter registration, and financial data outside statutory privacy and oversight requirements—a novel institutional workaround with no historical precedent in this dataset.

State-level institutions showed divergent trajectories: North Carolina's legislature overrode vetoes to expand ICE cooperation and cut voting access, while New York and Washington state courts and city governments (rent freeze, socialist mayors) pursued expansive protections.
oddities_or_open_questions: The same week produced both a Supreme Court ruling protecting birthright citizenship and a DOJ directive to prosecute 'birth tourism' as fraud—effectively attempting to circumvent the ruling through prosecutorial discretion; the durability of this workaround merits tracking.

Financial disclosures reveal Trump personally profited roughly $2.3 billion while everyday crypto investors in his ventures lost a comparable amount—raising unaddressed questions about market manipulation and whether any enforcement body has jurisdiction to investigate a sitting president's structured extraction from retail investors.

A uniformed active-duty Air Force officer publicly called for impeachment and was investigated but not prosecuted criminally, an unusual and unresolved test case for military speech rights amid a highly politicized environment.
sensor.summary: This week was defined by a landmark Supreme Court term that simultaneously checked and expanded executive power, alongside mounting evidence of systemic self-enrichment and institutional capture by the Trump White House. The Court struck down birthright-citizenship revocation and blocked an unlawful Fed governor removal, but in the same sitting overturned 90-year-old Humphrey's Executor protections, granting the president sweeping removal power over independent agencies—a structural shift toward unitary executive control. Simultaneously, financial disclosures revealed $2.2 billion in Trump family earnings (much from crypto ventures actively deregulated by the administration), a parallel White House-run internet infrastructure bypassing federal privacy law, and a Democratic-authored report alleging systemic corruption in the 250th-anniversary celebration. ICE conducted record-scale arrests, TPS protections were revoked for hundreds of thousands, and journalists and protesters faced detention. Judicial pushback (mail-ballot rulings, geofence warrant protections, USPS injunction) provided partial counterweight.
top_themes: Judicial mixed signals: the same term that reaffirmed birthright citizenship and blocked a Fed governor's illegal removal also gutted agency independence and campaign finance limits, producing genuinely contradictory pressure on democratic guardrails.

Presidential self-enrichment at scale: disclosures showing $2.2 billion in earnings, parallel White House-controlled data infrastructure, no-bid contracts, and family ties to federal contracts point to systemic monetization of the office.

Immigration enforcement escalation: record ICE arrests (10,000 in five days), TPS revocation for 350,000+ people, and prosecutorial targeting of birthright citizenship via 'birth tourism' fraud charges show an intensifying enforcement apparatus operating in the shadow of a Court ruling meant to constrain it.

Erosion of institutional guardrails via 'unitary executive' theory: the Slaughter ruling, National Design Studio's shadow IT infrastructure, and DOJ's rejection of ICC jurisdiction collectively signal a coordinated effort to insulate executive action from oversight.

Historical and civic memory contestation: government-funded 'Freedom Trucks' promoting sanitized history, a court ruling permitting removal of climate/slavery materials from parks, and grassroots counter-commemorations reveal an active battle over public memory around the 250th anniversary.
